techniques.title: CSPT chained with cache deception to account takeover
prereqs: A client-side path value reaches a fetch URL without encoding.
The API response is cacheable under a static-looking path.
The authenticated request carries a token the browser adds automatically.
steps: Find a fetch that builds a URL from a query, fragment, path, or stored value, for example `/v1/users/info/${userId}`.
Send `../` sequences in that value and observe whether the request reaches a different API route.
Look for a sensitive endpoint that becomes cacheable when it ends in `.css`, `.js`, `.png`, or another static extension.
Chain the CSPT into that endpoint so the victim's browser sends the authenticated request and the CDN caches the response.
Fetch the cached URL as an anonymous user and compare it with the victim's data.
techniques.proof: An unauthenticated request returns the victim's token or personal data from the cache. Show the CSPT URL, the authenticated cache fill, and the anonymous read.

techniques.title: Client-side path traversal to CSRF
prereqs: A front-end request path is attacker-controlled.
The request carries cookies and a CSRF header the front end adds.
A state-changing API route shares the same origin and method.
steps: Map every fetch/XHR sink and the HTTP method it uses.
Inject `../` to reroute the request to a state-changing route while keeping the front end's headers.
Test GET, POST, PATCH, PUT, and DELETE sinks; a GET sink can be chained with an upload or file-read gadget to control the next request.
Deliver the crafted page URL to a session you own and verify the state change.
Do not test destructive actions on a real account; use a test object and revert it.
techniques.proof: The victim's browser performs the state change with the site's own CSRF token. Record both the crafted URL and the changed server state.

techniques.title: ORM leak through relational filter traversal
prereqs: A user-controlled filter field or lookup reaches `QuerySet.filter`.
Sensitive model fields are reachable through a relation.
A response-length, status, or timing oracle exists.
steps: Identify filter parameters such as `filter`, `search`, `q`, `ordering`, or `where`.
Try a field that should be forbidden: `password`, `api_key`, `reset_token`.
Traverse relations with Django's double underscore: `created_by__password__startswith=a`.
Use a boolean or length oracle and extract one character at a time; stop at the first proven prefix.
Check `ordering` and `distinct` too; they can leak field values through sort order.
techniques.proof: A response changes only when the guessed prefix of a sensitive field is correct. Capture the two requests that differ.

techniques.title: Prisma operator injection and ORM leak
prereqs: A JSON, form, or cookie value is passed to a Prisma `where` without type validation.
The endpoint returns different errors or lengths for matches.
steps: Change a scalar to an object: `{"resetToken": {"not": "x"}}` or `{"contains": "a"}`.
Try URL-encoded and cookie variants: `resetToken[not]=x` and `Cookie: resetToken=j:{"not":"x"}`.
Use `contains` when `not` matches too many rows; binary-search a token or password prefix.
For time-based leaks, use `plormber` with a bounded request rate.
Stop at the first authenticated session or one sensitive field.
techniques.proof: An object where a string was expected changes the query result, or a reset/authentication flow succeeds without the real token.

techniques.title: Beego and OData filter-parser bypass
prereqs: A filter expression parser accepts a field and an operator.
A deny-list protects sensitive fields.
The API exposes `$filter`, `$expand`, or `q`.
steps: Try the denied field directly to establish the baseline block.
For Beego, test `email__password__startswith`; `parseExprs` may overwrite the first segment.
For OData, retrieve `/$metadata`, look for related entity sets, and use `$expand` on an association.
If `startswith`/`contains` are disabled, use `gt`/`lt` comparisons and the database collation order to binary-search the value.
Account for case-insensitive collations; use `tolower` or a case-sensitive operator where available.
techniques.proof: A deny-list bypass returns a different result for the sensitive field. Show the metadata, the filter, and the oracle.

techniques.title: Error-based and boolean-error SSTI
prereqs: User input reaches a template engine.
Output is not directly reflected, or only errors are visible.
steps: Send the universal probe `(1/0).zxy.zxy` and compare the error signature across engines.
For Jinja2, force the evaluated value into an attribute name: `{{getattr('', (...).__subclasses__())}}`; the AttributeError may contain the data.
For Twig, use `{{include(system('id'))}}`; the template-not-found error may contain the command output.
When errors are not verbose, use a conditional division by zero as a boolean oracle and extract one bit at a time.
Confirm with a harmless command or file read, never a destructive payload.
techniques.proof: The error text or the boolean oracle changes with the injected expression. Capture the baseline and the evaluated result.

techniques.title: Unicode normalization WAF bypass
prereqs: A WAF blocks a payload and the backend accepts Unicode.
The WAF and the backend use different normalization forms.
steps: Identify the WAF and the backend stack from headers and error pages.
Try fullwidth characters, compatibility forms, and overlong UTF-8 for the blocked token.
Try NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD differences, especially around quotes, slashes, and angle brackets.
Test Turkish `İ` and other case-mapping length changes against length-based validation.
Confirm the backend actually normalized the input into an executable form; a WAF bypass without execution is not a finding.
techniques.proof: The same semantic payload executes or traverses after normalization while the WAF allows it. Show both the blocked and bypassed requests.

techniques.title: Next.js data-request cache poisoning to stored XSS
prereqs: Pages Router with `getServerSideProps` on a non-dynamic route.
A request value is reflected in the page.
A shared cache or the framework cache stores the data response.
steps: Check for `__NEXT_DATA__` and the build id on a page.
Request the page with `?__nextDataReq=1`; if JSON is returned, the data route is exposed.
Add `x-now-route-matches: 1` and check whether `Cache-Control` changes from private to public.
Poison with a unique marker in a reflected header or cookie; fetch the clean URL without the marker.
If the clean response is HTML and contains the marker, escalate the marker to a script payload. Test on an unimportant route and never poison a production home page.
techniques.proof: A clean request returns attacker-controlled HTML from the cache. Record the poison request, the clean read, and the cache header.

techniques.title: HTTP/2 CONNECT stream tunneling
prereqs: The edge supports HTTP/2 CONNECT.
The proxy allows dynamic or unrestricted CONNECT targets.
steps: Establish one HTTP/2 connection to the proxy.
Open CONNECT streams to internal `IP:port` candidates over separate streams.
Read the HEADERS frame: `:status 200` suggests an open port; `503` plus `RST_STREAM` suggests closed.
Keep the scan small and read-only; do not send application payloads through a tunnel without explicit scope.
Correlate an open port with a known internal service before claiming impact.
techniques.proof: A multiplexed CONNECT stream reaches an internal service and returns a protocol response. Show the stream id and status.

techniques.title: ETag length cross-site leak
prereqs: The response ETag encodes the body length in hex.
The browser sends `If-None-Match` on repeat navigation.
The header size can cross the server's limit.
steps: Check whether the ETag matches `W/"<hex-size>-<hex-time>"`.
Find a page whose response size you can influence with CSRF-created padding.
Pad request headers to sit near the 16 KiB Node.js limit.
Navigate twice and measure `history.length`; a 431 replaces the history entry.
Use the length change as a one-bit oracle and binary-search a value you are authorised to read.
techniques.proof: A cross-site measurement changes only when the guessed value changes the response size. Prove the oracle with two controlled sizes.

techniques.title: Connection-pool ordering cross-origin leak
prereqs: Chrome's per-origin connection limit and host ordering are observable.
A cross-origin request encodes a secret in a hostname or redirect.
steps: Exhaust the connection pool with long-running requests.
Trigger the target's cross-origin request and a comparison request to a host you control.
Free one socket and observe which completes first.
Binary-search the hostname by alphabetical ordering.
Treat this as a privacy/identity oracle; do not use it to read data outside scope.
techniques.proof: A controlled comparison reveals one bit of the secret host or authentication state. Repeat enough trials to exclude noise.

techniques.title: SSRF response leak through redirect loops
prereqs: The server fetches an attacker URL and follows redirects.
Direct 200 responses are not returned to the attacker.
steps: Send a callback URL and count how many redirects the server follows.
Test 3xx statuses the client treats differently: 301-310, especially 305/306/309/310.
Run a loop that increments the status code and ends at a 200; some clients leak the full chain or the final body on an unhandled status.
Point the final hop at a controlled endpoint, then at an internal read-only endpoint only if scope allows.
Confirm the leaked body is server-side, not your own browser's response.
techniques.proof: The external response contains a redirect chain or final body fetched by the server. Capture the callback timestamps and the leaked response.

techniques.title: OAuth mutable claim takeover
prereqs: The client maps users by `email`, `preferred_username`, or another mutable claim.
The IdP lets a user control that claim without verification.
steps: Decode the ID token and compare `sub` with the claim used for account lookup.
Create an account on an IdP you control with the victim's email if the IdP allows unverified email.
Complete the OAuth flow and see whether the target logs you into the victim's account.
Try multiple IdPs and tenant types; a multi-tenant app may accept an external tenant.
Do not use a real victim's address; use a second account you own for the proof.
techniques.proof: The session lands on an account that belongs to your other identity, not the IdP subject you authenticated with.

techniques.title: OAuth client confusion
prereqs: The app accepts an access token from a user-controlled parameter or header.
It does not verify the token's client id or audience.
steps: Create a client you control on the same IdP and obtain a token for a user you own.
Send that token to the target's login or account-link endpoint.
If the target accepts it, check which account it maps to.
Try the token in a cookie, query, fragment, and JSON body; implicit-flow clients often accept all four.
Verify the token was issued for your client, not the target's.
techniques.proof: A token issued to a different client authenticates a session on the target. Record the token claims and the resulting session.

techniques.title: OAuth scope upgrade at the token endpoint
prereqs: The authorization server accepts a `scope` parameter during code exchange.
The issued token is not bound to the originally consented scope.
steps: Complete an authorization-code flow with a low-privilege scope.
Replay the code exchange with a higher-privilege `scope` value.
Inspect the access token or introspect it to see the granted scope.
Call a resource that requires the higher scope.
Repeat with a second client to see whether scope is bound to the client.
techniques.proof: The token endpoint issues a token with a scope the user never consented to, and the resource server honours it.

techniques.title: OAuth redirect_uri parser differential
prereqs: The authorization server validates `redirect_uri` with a prefix, regex, or origin-only check.
An allowed origin has an open redirect or user-controlled path.
steps: Register a client you own and observe the exact `redirect_uri` validation.
Try path traversal, extra slashes, `@`, encoded separators, and a subdomain you control.
If only the origin is checked, find an open redirect on that origin.
Capture the authorization code or token at your endpoint.
Exchange the code with the client's PKCE verifier or secret only if you own the client.
techniques.proof: The authorization server redirects to a host you control with a valid code or token. Show the exact `redirect_uri` and the callback.

techniques.title: SCIM attribute manipulation to account takeover
prereqs: SCIM provisioning is reachable with a token you can obtain or influence.
SCIM `userName`, `emails`, or group IDs map to internal identity fields.
steps: Find `/scim/v2/Users`, `/Groups`, and `/Bulk`; read the schema and auth model.
Try an unauthenticated request first; some libraries ship without auth.
As an authorised tenant admin, create or update a user you own and watch which internal fields change.
Test `userName`/`email` changes without the normal verification flow.
Test group `id` or `displayName` values that collide with internal role names.
Check whether a deprovisioned user is re-provisioned by any unrelated update.
techniques.proof: A SCIM write changes an internal identity or role that the UI would protect. Prove it with two accounts you own.

techniques.title: SCIM JSON interoperability bypass
prereqs: The SCIM implementation uses multiple JSON parsers or a catch-all PATCH branch.
`path` is optional for add/replace operations.
steps: Send a PATCH with `Operations[].path` omitted and a `value` object that targets a protected attribute.
Test duplicate keys, different Unicode escapes, and content-type changes across parsers.
Test `Bulk` ordering and circular references for a check-then-act gap.
Compare what the validator sees with what the user store persists.
Confirm the changed attribute is used for authorization, not only displayed.
techniques.proof: A protected attribute changes through a syntax the validator did not inspect. Show both parses and the persisted value.

techniques.title: MCP OAuth discovery and audience confusion
prereqs: An MCP server uses OAuth discovery and dynamic client registration.
The authorization server does not bind `aud` or `resource` to the MCP server.
steps: Read `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` and `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`.
Register a client and request a token for a low-privilege resource.
Replay the token against a different MCP server that shares the same authorization server.
Test whether a token for one resource is accepted by another; check scope namespace collisions.
Test whether a high-risk tool can be invoked without a per-action consent step.
techniques.proof: A token minted for one resource invokes tools on another, or a low-privilege token reaches a high-risk tool.

techniques.title: SAML parser differential and signature wrapping
prereqs: The SP accepts a SAML response from an IdP you can influence or a test IdP.
Validation and signature verification use different XML parsers.
steps: Capture a valid assertion and decode the base64 XML.
Try signature stripping, XSW1-XSW8, and comment injection in NameID.
Test namespace and entity differences between the validator and verifier.
Try a signed assertion from a different audience or IdP.
Replay the assertion within its validity window.
techniques.proof: The SP creates a session for a NameID that was not in the signed assertion, or accepts an assertion for another audience.

techniques.title: GraphQL global-id and field-level authorization
prereqs: The API exposes `node(id:)` or a similar global-id lookup.
The resolver checks the type but not the object owner.
steps: Introspect the schema and list every type, field, mutation, and deprecated field.
Decode a global id (`base64(Type:id)`), change the type or id, and re-encode.
Query the object as its owner, as a second account, and anonymously; request every field, not just the UI fields.
Test mutations with a swapped id and mass-assigned fields.
Try aliases and batching only for rate-limit analysis, not for data enumeration.
techniques.proof: A second account or anonymous caller receives fields or objects it should not see. Capture the introspection excerpt and the query.

techniques.title: Second-order and asynchronous IDOR
prereqs: An object id is stored by one request and used later by a worker, export, or notification.
The later job uses a different authorization context.
steps: Map write-then-process flows: imports, exports, reports, webhooks, emails, and PDF jobs.
Create a job under account A, then change the object or tenant id in the stored record.
Trigger the worker and read the result from account B.
Test parent ids, nested ids, and batch ids, not only the top-level id.
Check whether a deleted or transferred object still resolves in the worker.
techniques.proof: Account B receives a report or notification containing account A's data. Show the write, the trigger, and the cross-account read.

techniques.title: Mass assignment on optional and nested fields
prereqs: A profile or object update accepts a JSON body.
The server binds more fields than the UI sends.
steps: Capture the legitimate update and diff it against the object schema.
Add fields one at a time: `role`, `is_admin`, `verified`, `tenant_id`, `owner_id`, `permissions`.
Try nested objects and arrays; a nested `organization.role` may bypass a top-level check.
Re-read the object with a fresh session and confirm the field persisted.
Check whether the field changes authorization, not just display.
techniques.proof: A field the UI never exposes changes server-side and alters access. Show the request, the persisted value, and the resulting permission.

techniques.title: Single-packet race on a state machine
prereqs: A check-then-act flow has no atomic constraint.
The state change is idempotent-looking but actually repeats.
steps: Model the invariant: balance, redemption count, vote count, or active session count.
Send 10-20 identical requests over one HTTP/2 connection with the last byte gated.
Compare the invariant before and after; stop at the first duplicate side effect.
Test partial failure: one success and one error after the side effect is still a race.
Revert state and record the timing window.
techniques.proof: The invariant changes more than once for a single intended action. Show the concurrent requests and the final state.

techniques.title: Cache deception through path normalization
prereqs: A CDN caches responses by extension or path while the origin ignores the suffix.
A private page is reachable with a static-looking suffix.
steps: Request a private page with `.css`, `.js`, `.png`, `%2f`, `;`, and trailing-slash variants.
Check `Cache-Control`, `X-Cache`, `Age`, and `Vary` on each variant.
Log in as account A, request the variant, then fetch it anonymously and as account B.
Test encoded separators and case variations; normalization often differs by layer.
Do not cache a real user's data on a shared edge without permission.
techniques.proof: A private response is served from the cache to a different session. Show the authenticated fill and the anonymous hit.

techniques.title: Host header poisoning of password reset
prereqs: The reset email builds an absolute URL from the request Host or `X-Forwarded-Host`.
The mailer does not use a fixed canonical origin.
steps: Request a reset for an account you own and capture the email link.
Change `Host`, `X-Forwarded-Host`, and `X-Forwarded-Server` to a host you control.
If the link changes, request a reset for a second owned account and confirm the token arrives at your host.
Check whether the token is valid on the real origin.
Do not request a reset for another user's account.
techniques.proof: The reset email contains an attacker-controlled origin and the token works on the real site. Show the request and the email.

techniques.title: JWT claim and key confusion
prereqs: A JWT controls identity, role, tenant, or audience.
The verifier accepts a key or algorithm you can influence.
steps: Decode the token and list every claim the server acts on.
Test `alg=none`, HS256 with the public key as the secret, and `kid` path traversal.
Point `jku`/`x5u` at a JWKS you control; check whether the server fetches it.
Change one claim at a time: `sub`, `role`, `tenant`, `aud`, `iss`.
A changed claim is only a finding when the server acts on it.
techniques.proof: The server accepts a token with a changed claim or a key it should not trust, and the session gains the corresponding access.

techniques.title: MFA step skip and OTP race
prereqs: The password step issues a session before the second factor.
The MFA check is a separate endpoint, not a middleware gate.
steps: After the password step, call a sensitive endpoint directly without completing MFA.
Inspect cookies for a `verified` flag or a second token.
Replay the same OTP twice and race two verifications.
Test backup codes and SMS fallback for weaker rate limits.
Check whether a password reset or email change skips the second factor.
techniques.proof: A session reaches post-MFA functionality without a valid second factor, or one OTP creates two sessions.

techniques.title: File upload polyglot to execution
prereqs: An upload accepts a file that is later served or processed.
The extension, MIME, or magic-byte check is incomplete.
steps: Map the upload field, size limit, storage path, and serving URL.
Test double extension, case, trailing dot/space, null byte, and `.htaccess`/`web.config`.
Add a valid image header to a script and check whether the server re-encodes or stores raw bytes.
Request the stored file and see whether the handler executes it.
Prove execution with `id` or a DNS callback only on a lab or authorised host.
techniques.proof: The uploaded file executes server-side code or is served as active HTML/JS to another user. Show the upload, path, and response.

techniques.title: Deserialization gadget chain
prereqs: The app deserializes a client-controlled value.
A library with a usable gadget is on the classpath.
steps: Recognise the format: PHP `O:`, Java `AC ED`, Python pickle, .NET `AAEAAAD`, Ruby Marshal.
Round-trip the value unchanged; if accepted, you control the object.
Enumerate libraries and versions from headers, errors, and dependencies.
Choose a callback or file-read gadget first; avoid destructive commands.
Prove the effect server-side, not only in a local harness.
techniques.proof: A benign gadget produces a DNS callback or a controlled file read on the server. Show the payload and the server-side effect.

techniques.title: Cloud metadata SSRF to identity
prereqs: A server-side fetch reaches an internal address.
The workload has a cloud identity.
steps: Confirm the fetch with a unique callback.
Try AWS IMDSv1, then the IMDSv2 token flow; GCP with `Metadata-Flavor: Google`; Azure with `Metadata: true`.
Read only the identity document or the shortest credential path.
Use the credential for one read-only identity call; do not create resources.
If IMDSv2 blocks you, look for a proxy or header-forging path instead of brute force.
techniques.proof: A metadata response returns a role name or token that you can use for one read-only call. Show the request and the identity.

techniques.title: Subdomain takeover chained to OAuth
prereqs: A dangling CNAME or unclaimed service hostname exists in scope.
The hostname is an allowed OAuth redirect or cookie domain.
steps: Enumerate CNAMEs and check for provider 404s or unclaimed buckets.
Claim the resource only on a provider and hostname the programme authorises.
Check whether the hostname is registered as an OAuth `redirect_uri` or a cookie domain.
Complete an OAuth flow through the claimed host and capture the code.
Do not impersonate the brand or collect real user data.
techniques.proof: The claimed host receives an OAuth code or a session cookie scoped to the parent domain. Show the DNS record and the callback.

techniques.title: Client-side prototype pollution to DOM XSS
prereqs: A merge, clone, or query parser writes attacker keys into `Object.prototype`.
A gadget later reads the polluted property into a sink.
steps: Find recursive merges, `Object.assign`, lodash `merge`, and query parsers.
Inject `__proto__[x]=y`, `constructor[prototype][x]=y`, and JSON `{"__proto__":{"x":"y"}}`.
Search for gadgets that read the polluted key into `innerHTML`, `srcdoc`, `href`, or `eval`.
Prove execution in the browser with a benign marker.
Check server-side pollution separately; it may reach a template or child process.
techniques.proof: A polluted property reaches a sink and executes in the browser. Show the pollution source and the sink.

techniques.title: Unkeyed-header cache poisoning
prereqs: A reverse proxy caches by path but forwards an unkeyed header.
The origin reflects that header into a link, redirect, or script.
steps: Find cache headers and a cacheable page.
Send a unique marker in `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Scheme`, and `X-Original-URL`.
Request the clean URL without the header; if the marker persists, the cache is poisoned.
Escalate the marker to a redirect or script only on a test path.
Purge or wait out the cache and never poison a production login page.
techniques.proof: A clean request returns the attacker's marker from the cache. Show the poison and the clean hit.

techniques.title: CI/CD expression injection to secret exfiltration
prereqs: A workflow interpolates attacker-controlled event text into a `run:` block or an env file.
The job has secrets or a write token.
steps: Read `.github/workflows/*.yml`; grep for `${{ github.event.* }}` inside `run:` and `$GITHUB_ENV`/`$GITHUB_PATH`.
Check the trigger: `issues`, `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target`, and `workflow_run` are externally reachable.
Follow `uses:` into composite actions; the sink may live in another repository.
Confirm secrets reachable by the job and the token permissions.
Prove with a callback from a fork or a test repo you own; do not exfiltrate real secrets.
techniques.proof: A workflow run you triggered sends a callback or writes a marker using the job's token. Show the workflow, trigger, and callback.

techniques.title: Indirect prompt injection to tool exfiltration
prereqs: The assistant reads documents, web pages, or tickets you can influence.
It has a fetch, email, or tool-call capability.
steps: Map the retrieval sources and every tool the assistant can call.
Place a unique instruction in a document the assistant summarises: ask it to fetch a URL you control.
Check whether the tool call happens without confirmation and whether data is included in the URL.
Test cross-user retrieval with two accounts you own.
Test invisible Unicode tags for instructions hidden from human reviewers.
techniques.proof: The assistant follows injected content and sends data or a request to your endpoint. Show the document, the model output, and the callback.

techniques.title: Mobile OAuth custom-scheme hijack
prereqs: The app receives OAuth codes through a custom scheme.
Another app can register a broader or matching intent filter.
steps: Decompile the APK and read the manifest for `BROWSABLE` intent filters and custom schemes.
Check whether the redirect uses a verified App Link or a bare custom scheme.
Build a test app with a broader filter for the same scheme and see whether it receives the code.
Verify whether PKCE is enforced; without it, the intercepted code is exchangeable.
Use only your own test accounts and device.
techniques.proof: A second app receives the authorization code, and the code can be exchanged. Show the manifest, the interception, and the token.

techniques.title: APK secret to live API access
prereqs: An authorised APK is available.
It embeds a key, endpoint, or signing material.
steps: Decompile with jadx and decode resources with apktool.
Grep for URLs, cloud keys, JWTs, Firebase config, and basic-auth strings.
Classify each secret and its scope; do not use it beyond a read-only check.
Replay the mobile request with the extracted key and a test account.
Confirm the server accepts it and returns data or an action the user should not have.
techniques.proof: The extracted credential authenticates to the live service and returns data or an action. Show the static string and the live request.
